newsitem.title: FRANCE: "No reason to be afraid of Europe" - Kohl.
newsitem.headline: "No reason to be afraid of Europe" - Kohl.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met French President Jacques Chirac on Saturday for a mixture of political talks on European Union issues and a family dinner at a provincial French gastronomic fair.

The pretext for the first of four meetings Kohl and Chirac will have in the next two weeks was the award of a French culinary literature prize to the chancellor's wife, Hannelore, for her best-selling book "Gastronomic Journey through Germany".

But Kohl used the opportunity to convey a political message to the French, torn by fresh debate over the planned European single currency and its impact on sluggish economic growth and record unemployment in France.
"There is no reason to be pessimistic. There is no reason to be afraid of Europe," Kohl told reporters at a brief photo session with Chirac before they dined together with their wives.
"Food and wine are part of the joy of living that is necessary, especially at a moment when pessimism is spreading considerably in Europe," the chancellor said.
He stressed that a more united Europe would not be grey and uniform but would retain its diversity.

"We Germans and French are right in the middle of this enterprise, not because we are necessarily the strongest but because we have fought longest for this enterprise. It is our duty to succeed," he said.
He said he was happy to be able to write a new page in the history of European integration with Chirac.
"Of course, there will be difficulties. But difficulties are made to be overcome and we will succeed," Kohl said.
French officials said in advance of the meeting they did not expect any policy statement to be issued.

Paris and Bonn agree in principle on the need for a stability pact to limit the budget deficits of the EU countries which qualify for a single currency in 1999 and impose sanctions on those who exceed the targets.

But France opposes Germany's insistance on putting strict figures on exceptions that may be allowed, and Prime Minister Alain Juppe reasserted on Wednesday the French view that elected political authorities, not the future European central bank, must set European economic policies for growth and employment.
A call by former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing for a depreciation of the franc to revive the economy, rejected by both Paris and Bonn, has added to tension between the two countries.
Kohl travels to France again on Tuesday for a regular working dinner with Chirac in Paris, and the two men will meet in Nuremberg, Germany, on December 9 for a twice-yearly Franco-German summit.
In Nuremberg, they are expected to announce a joint initiative on reform of European Union institutions ahead of an EU summit in Dublin on December 13 and 14.
